saturation_history.rationale: Not tested: the taxonomy was generated from this minibatch.

uncovered_concepts: Closest in-sync replica for Git reads
Priority scheduling for user-initiated reference updates
Virtualized filesystem for very large repositories
Partial-clone interface for on-demand object retrieval
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers replica count, commit coordination, authority, request placement, planned maintenance, and high-level client background maintenance or Scalar-to-core-Git integration. However, the minibatch introduces several distinct architectural axes that those dimensions cannot absorb without conflation: repository storage and access architecture (packfile locality, dedicated fileservers, RPC versus distributed or block-level filesystems, and local caching); replication implementation and topology (application-level versus filesystem replication, Git/rsync mechanisms, geographic placement, rack anti-colocation, voting roles, read-replica selection, failure detection, and automated repair); reference-update scheduling and coalescing; and client-side repository materialization and metadata strategies (virtualized filesystems, sparse checkout, partial clones, fetch-object separation, index representation, and filesystem watching). The three-replica count and majority-style commitment themselves fit existing replication-factor and coordination dimensions, while workload ratios, latency budgets, and measured performance effects are constraints or outcomes rather than missing decision axes.

uncovered_concepts: GVFS protocol for large repositories and user groups
Git protocol with Scalar registration as infrastructure-light fallback
GVFS deployment without a cache server for small repositories
saturation_history.rationale: The minibatch is not fully saturated. Most codes are covered by existing dimensions: WAL authority, push consistency and acknowledgement map to Authority Synchronization and Replica Commit Coordination; plain Git repositories, data transformation, and local NVMe storage map to Repository Storage Representation; sparse checkout and Scalar maintenance map to Client Clone Materialization and Client Maintenance Execution; and quiescence, rolling reboots, rack isolation, and failure recovery are already represented. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct client workspace-layout decision covering separation of the repository/working directory from sibling build outputs; a transfer-serving and cache-topology decision covering GVFS versus Git protocol and when a co-located cache is used; a repository-object replication decision covering packfile fan-out and its deliberate separation from reference-transaction synchronization; and a collaboration/control-model decision covering distributed Git workflows versus centralized repository hosting. These are relevant architectural axes and cannot be added as values to the existing dimensions without conflating distinct decisions.

The taxonomy covers background maintenance in general, repository storage representation, replica checksums for cross-replica equivalence, and automated replica repair, but it does not capture the distinct packfile-maintenance design space: incremental versus full repacking, multi-pack-index-based reference redirection, and deferred deletion of obsolete packs. The associated pack-count and storage-footprint effects are also not represented. Per-repository checksum tracking is additionally distinct from the existing replica checksum strategy because it detects corruption of individual on-disk copies for health management rather than verifying equivalent logical state across replicas. The remaining codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: client configuration and Scalar/core-Git integration, partial cloning, replica topology and quorum coordination, repository placement, failure detection/failover, and repository serving architecture.

Most open codes are covered by existing dimensions: Git object and packfile representations, DAG-related lookup costs, and distributed-store alternatives fit Repository Storage Representation; foreground versus incremental/background maintenance fits Client Maintenance Execution; replica voting, durability, repair, and failure-aware routing fit Replica Commit Coordination and Replica Failure Recovery; and WAL persistence, acknowledgment, linearizable publication, and local-repository synchronization fit Authority Synchronization. The clear gap is distributing a single repository across multiple disks or machines (repository sharding/partitioning). Existing dimensions cover placing whole repository replicas and accessing dedicated fileservers, but do not capture the distinct decision of partitioning one repository's data across machines to obtain parallelism and availability.

Most open codes are subsumed by existing dimensions: WAL persistence and S3-based authority are covered by Authority Synchronization; gossip, direct S3 catch-up, and compacted-pack distribution fit Repository Replication Mechanism; elastic replica counts and idle-replica removal fit Replica Topology and Factor and Warm-cache Materialization; fsmonitor and selective path inspection fit Client Working-State Monitoring; GVFS, sparse checkout, on-demand objects, and cache servers fit Client Clone Materialization and Repository Serving Architecture; and packfile, multi-pack-index, incremental-compaction, and primary-only repacking choices fit Packfile Lifecycle Management. Replica locking, round-trip latency, and overlapping waits are covered by the existing commit, authority, and latency dimensions. However, the taxonomy lacks a decision axis for validating replica read readiness against an authoritative version token (including conditional ETag reads and S3-verified reads); checksum strategy is not equivalent to this freshness/read-admission protocol. It also lacks a lifecycle dimension for compacting the authoritative WAL itself: existing packfile lifecycle management concerns Git object packs, while periodic WAL compaction addresses restore cost and unbounded log growth.

values.description: Uses Scalar as an additional client mechanism for achieving required large-repository performance.

values.label: Core Git performance capabilities
values.description: Moves repository management and performance features into the core Git client.

values.label: Additional Git management layers
values.description: The longer-term design rejects continued dependence on management layers such as Scalar above core Git.

values.label: Scalar-to-core-Git transition
values.description: Treats Scalar as a transitional solution while equivalent capabilities become available in core Git.

values.label: Scalar configuration tuning
values.description: Applying recommended Git configuration values to accelerate client commands.

values.label: GVFS Protocol in standard Git
values.description: Is the GVFS Protocol integrated into the standard Git client?

values.label: Reliability-performance-scale platform objectives
values.description: The client integration direction targets improved reliability, performance, and scale for Git operations.

values.label: Low-friction platform migration
values.description: Adoption of improved repository infrastructure minimizes migration disruption.

values.label: Incremental infrastructure evolution
values.description: Version-control infrastructure continues evolving as workload and platform conditions change.

values.label: Agent-driven workload growth
values.description: Software agents increase code, pull-request, and CI workload demands on repository infrastructure.

values.label: Repository availability productivity impact
values.description: Repository unavailability directly reduces developer and CI productivity.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Topology and Factor
selected_clusters.description: How many replicas and what physical topology provide repository redundancy and failure isolation?

values.label: Rack-level replica anti-colocation
values.description: Placing repository replicas in different racks to isolate rack-wide failures.

values.label: Distant replica placement
values.description: Placing replicas across geographically separated locations despite inter-replica latency.

values.label: Colocated filesystem replicas
values.description: Keeping filesystem replicas near one another because block replication is latency-sensitive.

values.label: Block-level filesystem replication
values.description: Replicating repository storage at filesystem or block level.

values.label: Three replicas per repository
values.description: Maintaining three repository copies as the selected replication factor.

values.label: Non-voting geo-replication replicas
values.description: Keeping geographically replicated hosts out of write-voting quorums so writes survive their temporary unavailability.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica allocation
values.description: Replica counts vary with repository demand, from minimal availability to large read-serving pools.

values.label: Geographically localized replica reads
values.description: Serving reads from synchronized replicas near users to improve transfer locality.

values.label: Durable highly available content access
values.description: Maintaining durable, highly available repository and gist access through multi-copy replication.

values.label: Replication floor and capacity ceiling
values.description: The fixed replication floor is costly for small repositories while offering insufficient serving capacity for massive repositories.

values.label: Two-copy repository state after sudden loss
values.description: Leaves a repository with two surviving copies after an unexpected server disappearance, preserving service but reducing failure tolerance.

values.label: Replica-count scaling bottleneck
values.description: Increasing the number of replicas reduces push throughput under three-phase commit.

selected_clusters.name: Authority Synchronization
selected_clusters.description: Which mechanism coordinates authoritative repository state persistence and synchronization?

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead log
values.description: Persisting authoritative repository updates through a write-ahead log in S3.

values.label: S3 compare-and-swap synchronization
values.description: Uses atomic S3 compare-and-swap operations to serialize concurrent write-ahead-log updates.

values.label: WAL-based repository consistency
values.description: Uses a write-ahead log as the authoritative record for consistent repository operations without an external relational database.

values.label: Push acknowledgment after WAL persistence
values.description: Acknowledges pushes only after their complete operation is durable in the authoritative log.

values.label: Fully consistent repository views
values.description: Maintains every accessed repository view as fully consistent rather than partially consistent.

values.label: External relational database for repository references
values.description: Stores repository references in an external relational database alongside blob-stored packfiles.

values.label: Consensus-free repository primaries
values.description: Allows any server to receive updates instead of using elections or fixed primary ownership.

values.label: Repository copies as consensus source
values.description: What repository state establishes consensus for replicated operations?

values.label: Cloud-agnostic object-storage deployment
values.description: The authority log runs on S3-compatible object storage across cloud providers.

values.label: Batched WAL uploads
values.description: Multiple pushes are grouped to avoid one object-store write per push.

values.label: One-object-store-write-per-push ingestion
values.description: Each push is ingested with a separate object-store write.

values.label: Single-local-repository reference synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize with one local repository instead of a replica quorum.

values.label: Periodic WAL compaction
values.description: The write-ahead log is periodically compacted to bound restore cost and retained history.

values.label: Compaction results recorded across storage representations
values.description: Compaction outcomes are recorded for both the WAL and on-disk repository so replicas reproduce them.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone deployment
values.description: High-performance clusters use a lower-latency object-storage tier for WAL updates and push ingestion.

values.label: ETag-conditional read verification
values.description: Replicas use conditional object-storage reads to verify WAL-index freshness before serving fetches or clones.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Serving Architecture
selected_clusters.description: How does the application access repository storage across serving and storage nodes?

values.label: Stateless repository-serving cluster
values.description: Treats local repository copies as replaceable warm caches and avoids authoritative server-local repository state.

values.label: RPC-based repository access
values.description: Accessing repositories remotely through an application-facing RPC layer.

values.label: Dedicated repository fileservers
values.description: Storing repositories on dedicated fileservers rather than a shared distributed filesystem.

values.label: Co-located GVFS cache server
values.description: Places a cache server with the repository to handle many GVFS protocol requests.

values.label: Git protocol with Scalar registration
values.description: Uses ordinary Git protocol and client registration when GVFS cache infrastructure is unavailable.

values.label: GVFS without cache server
values.description: Uses GVFS protocol without a dedicated cache server for repositories small enough not to require one.

values.label: Horizontal application-server replication
values.description: How does the serving application scale its application instances around repository access?

values.label: Warm-cache materialization
values.description: Recreates absent local repositories from the S3 write-ahead log when routing directs work to another node.

values.label: Single-machine repository storage
values.description: Keeping each repository on only one machine after remote fileserver access.

values.label: Git hosting operational difficulty
values.description: Makes repository hosting operations a significant scalability and reliability concern.

values.label: Read-dominant repository workload
values.description: Operating under a workload with roughly one hundred reads per write.

selected_clusters.name: Client Clone Materialization
selected_clusters.description: How are repository content and working-tree data materialized on large-repository clients?

values.label: Partial-clone object materialization
values.description: Fetching missing repository objects on demand instead of storing every reachable object locally.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem materialization
values.description: Using a virtualized filesystem to support very large repositories without fully materializing content.

values.label: Sparse-checkout materialization
values.description: Populating only selected working-tree paths to control client materialization size.

values.label: GVFS-protocol cloning
values.description: Cloning through the GVFS hosting protocol for large repositories.

values.label: Nested source working directory
values.description: Places the working tree beneath the repository directory to separate source files from adjacent build outputs.

values.label: Reduced Git working-directory management load
values.description: Separating build outputs from the working directory reduces the work Git performs while managing repository files.

values.label: Reduced object-transfer burden
values.description: Partial transfer and caching reduce client data movement and central-server load compared with complete object database transfer.

values.label: Populated-file data cost
values.description: Populating working files costs substantially more data movement and processing than changing index entries.

values.label: Populated-file modification-detection cost
values.description: Determining modifications across many populated files becomes an important client scalability cost.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Storage Representation
selected_clusters.description: Which repository object representation and access pattern supports server-scale Git workloads?

values.label: Size-minimizing packfile layout
values.description: Organizing packed objects primarily to minimize storage size, accepting physical indirection and random reads.

values.label: Whole-file local caching
values.description: Caching an entire repository file locally to make random access acceptable.

values.label: Distributed filesystem architecture
values.description: Distributing repository storage through a shared filesystem.

values.label: Plain Git repositories on local NVMe
values.description: Stores ordinary Git repositories on local NVMe to support random packfile reads and standard client access.

values.label: Normal on-disk Git repository operations
values.description: Runs standard Git operations against ordinary on-disk repositories using upstream-compatible tooling.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository replicas
values.description: Allows replicas to expose newly pushed repository data only after propagation completes.

values.label: Content-addressable object storage
values.description: Repository objects are stored and addressed by content hashes.

values.label: DAG-dependent object traversal
values.description: Repository access follows dependent commit, tree, and file references sequentially.

values.label: Distributed key-value object storage
values.description: Git objects are mapped directly onto a distributed key-value store.

values.label: Distributed hash-table packfile storage
values.description: Normal on-disk packfiles are replaced by a distributed hash table.

values.label: Packfile-based network transfer
values.description: Git transfers repository changes through packfiles over the network.

values.label: Distributed identical repository instances
values.description: Hosting servers and developer machines retain the same distributed repository model.

values.label: Packfile-based repository storage
values.description: Repository code and metadata are stored in compressed filesystem packfiles.

values.label: Single on-disk HTTP repository
values.description: An HTTP daemon serves one local on-disk repository.

values.label: Server-internal non-packfile storage
values.description: The server uses an internal representation other than packfiles while preserving packfile network operations.

values.label: Multi-machine repository placement
values.description: Repository data is distributed across multiple disks and machines for parallelism and availability.

values.label: Efficient Git cloning
values.description: Preserves efficient cloning by retaining plain Git data rather than transforming it for clients.

values.label: Network-filesystem performance and correctness problems
values.description: What operational effect results when Git repositories are exposed through networked filesystem semantics?

values.label: Distributed-store access overhead
values.description: Object-level distributed storage adds repeated network round trips and latency.

values.label: Unacceptable clone performance
values.description: Object-level distribution makes repository cloning too slow for practical use.

values.label: Packfile hosting management burden
values.description: Large binary packfiles make filesystem-scale repository management difficult.

values.label: Packfile hosting scalability ceiling
values.description: Packfile-based hosting limits availability and scalability for large providers.

selected_clusters.name: Packfile Lifecycle Management
selected_clusters.description: How are Git packfiles repacked, indexed, retained, and removed over time?

values.label: Incremental pack-file repacking
values.description: Which pack-maintenance strategy limits each repacking operation while reducing large repositories’ pack count?

values.label: Multi-pack-index reference redirection
values.description: Which index mechanism redirects selected objects to newly generated packs while retaining old packs temporarily?

values.label: Deferred obsolete-pack deletion
values.description: When are obsolete pack files deleted relative to pack creation and reference updates?

values.label: Single-pack-file repacking
values.description: Accumulated packfiles are rewritten into one packfile as a maintenance strategy unsuitable for very large repositories.

values.label: Primary-only compaction
values.description: Only the primary replica performs repository compaction, while replicas consume the recorded result.

values.label: Replica-side repository repacking
values.description: Replicas independently trigger repository repacking as opposed to consuming primary-produced compacted data.

values.label: Unbounded pack-file accumulation
values.description: What pack-growth condition can result when pack maintenance is not bounded?

values.label: Pack-count and storage-footprint reduction
values.description: What storage result follows from incremental repacking and obsolete-pack expiration?

values.label: Git compaction as ingestion bottleneck
values.description: At high throughput, on-disk Git compaction becomes the limiting factor for repository ingestion.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Failure Recovery
selected_clusters.description: How are failed or retiring replica servers detected and repaired to restore repository redundancy?

values.label: Live-traffic-based failure detection
values.description: Detecting server failure from live application traffic and routing requests around unavailable servers.

values.label: Automated permanent-failure repair
values.description: Automatically restoring repository replication after disk or server failures.

values.label: Retiring-server replica-count removal
values.description: Removing a retiring server from active replica counts while keeping it available until repairs complete.

values.label: MxN failure-detection matrix
values.description: How are failure observations distributed across application servers and file servers?

values.label: Per-application-server failure isolation
values.description: How are failure classifications isolated when one application server has a local connectivity or DNS fault?

values.label: Heartbeat-based primary failure detection
values.description: Which mechanism is used as the primary detector for failed repository servers?

values.label: Advisory replica-offline status
values.description: How is an uncertain offline judgment represented in replica routing?

values.label: Cross-server fault inference
values.description: How are file-server faults distinguished from application-server faults?

values.label: Pet-style repository operations
values.description: Are repositories managed as individually irreplaceable assets or interchangeable instances?

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: A replica is marked offline only after three consecutive request failures.

values.label: Losing-replica isolation
values.description: Replicas on the losing side of a write vote are removed from reads and writes until repaired.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: Replacement replicas can be created anywhere from either surviving repository copy.

values.label: Localized failure-detector false positive
values.description: What failure-detection error can remain localized to one application server?

values.label: Operational burden of repository health management
values.description: What operational effect follows from continuous repository location, checksum, corruption, and repair management?

values.label: Cluster-size recovery scaling
values.description: Replica recovery accelerates as the file-server cluster grows.

values.label: Replica failover from concurrent maintenance
values.description: Concurrent maintenance on multiple replica nodes can trigger repository failover and availability impact.

selected_clusters.name: Version-Control Operating Model
selected_clusters.description: Which collaboration and repository-control model governs how users and teams exchange Git changes?

values.label: Distributed version-control model
values.description: Retains decentralized repositories and offline change exchange as the underlying version-control model.

values.label: Decentralized subsystem-maintainer workflow
values.description: Organizes development through many maintainers and decentralized subsystem ownership.

values.label: Offline work and delayed-push capabilities
values.description: Provides offline development and postpones synchronization with the central host.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: Coordinates users through a centralized repository host despite distributed client capabilities.

values.label: Central-server-coupled object retrieval
values.description: Clients rely on a central server for missing objects, relaxing the fully distributed collaboration model.

values.label: Distributed-model mismatch with centralized workflows
values.description: Creates friction when organizations use centralized coordination rather than decentralized development.

dropped_dimensions.rationale: Not a decision point: 1 candidate decision(s) (accepted/rejected/mixed values) besides outcomes; at least 2 required.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions relevant to scaling Git across many repositories, users, servers, and clients, such as replica topology (9), storage representation (20), packfile lifecycle (21), and client materialization (12). However, Client Scaling Integration (8) overlaps Client Configuration and Registration (32): value 8.6, "Scalar configuration tuning," answers the configuration question and should move to dimension 32. Authority Synchronization (10) also partially overlaps Replica Commit Coordination (25), since WAL/CAS and consensus or commit protocols all describe how replicated updates are coordinated; keep the questions separate but reassign values so 10 contains authoritative-log persistence/synchronization and 25 contains replica transaction ordering and publication. These are limited overlaps rather than a pervasive collapse of the taxonomy.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions use explicit question-like names and most values have distinct labels, such as 25.1 Three-phase commit versus 25.2 Majority-based write commitment. However, several descriptions do not state the decision or alternative clearly: dimension 5 Repository Placement Strategy says only that documents vary rather than naming the placement question; dimension 8 Client Scaling Integration mixes integration choices with configuration, objectives, and outcomes; and dimension 31 Client Filesystem and Status Monitoring includes 31.3 Performance bottleneck tracing, which is not covered by its stated watching/status scope. Several values also retain question-shaped descriptions instead of distinguishing the option, notably 10.8 Repository copies as consensus source, 11.7 Horizontal application-server replication, 14.4 MxN failure-detection matrix, and 21.1–21.3. Rename dimension 5 to an explicit placement-and-rematerialization question, move 8.6 Scalar configuration tuning to dimension 32, rename dimension 31 to include performance monitoring or drop 31.3, and replace the question-shaped value descriptions with the corresponding existing option wording.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents the major server-side and client-side scaling areas with multiple candidate decisions in each: replication and coordination (25, 17, 26), placement and topology (5, 9), authority and serving architecture (10, 11), storage and packfile lifecycle (20, 21), failure recovery and maintenance (14, 6), and client cloning, fetching, maintenance, indexing, monitoring, and configuration (12, 22, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32). Even the narrower dimensions 18 and 32 provide two candidate decisions. No major use-case area lacks a decision point with several candidate values.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy is strongly in scope for the stated use case: dimensions such as 9 Replica Topology and Factor, 10 Authority Synchronization, 17 Repository Replication Mechanism, 20 Repository Storage Representation, 21 Packfile Lifecycle Management, and 22/27/30/31 client scaling decisions directly address large repositories, many repositories, many users, server operations, and client operations. The main tangential area is dimension 15, Version-Control Operating Model: values such as 15.2 Decentralized subsystem-maintainer workflow and 15.6 Distributed-model mismatch with centralized workflows concern collaboration organization rather than architectural scaling decisions. Drop dimension 15, or move only 15.4 Centralized repository hosting and 15.5 Central-server-coupled object retrieval into the relevant serving/client dimensions and discard the remaining operating-model content.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Several values are catch-all buckets rather than focused alternatives. Drop 8.8 "Reliability-performance-scale platform objectives" and 8.10 "Incremental infrastructure evolution", which bundle broad platform goals and evolution concerns. Drop 31.3 "Performance bottleneck tracing", a generic diagnostic activity rather than a specific design alternative. Drop 14.14 "Operational burden of repository health management", which aggregates location, checksum, corruption, and repair concerns. Drop 20.18 "Network-filesystem performance and correctness problems", which combines broad consequences instead of representing one concrete option. The rest of the taxonomy contains many specific decision alternatives, so it is not dominated entirely by catch-alls.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many relevant decision candidates, but several dimensions bundle distinct decisions and several values are subtopics or questions rather than answers. Dimension 20, "Repository Storage Representation," combines packfile layout, object storage, filesystem architecture, access patterns, and network transfer; split it into separate existing-content decisions for storage representation and access/transfer architecture. Dimension 17, "Repository Replication Mechanism," includes lifecycle and recovery choices such as 17.8 "Direct S3 replica catch-up," 17.9 "Idle-replica removal and rematerialization," and 17.10 "S3 distribution of compacted packs"; move these to dimensions 10, 14, and 21 respectively. Dimension 25, "Replica Commit Coordination," includes the implementation optimization 25.7 "Overlapped coordinator work during network waits," which should be moved to the scheduling/implementation decision in dimension 18. Client dimensions 22, 27, 30, and 31 each combine multiple decisions (fetch exposure versus execution, scheduling versus execution, index representation versus caching, and filesystem watching versus status inspection); split each into separate questions while retaining their existing values. Finally, question-form values such as 8.7, 10.8, 11.7, and 14.4-14.9 should be rewritten or reorganized as concrete alternative answers rather than standalone questions.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Although several dimensions are well-formed decision questions with at least two candidates—such as 3 Replica Checksum Strategy, 18 Replica Update Scheduling, 22 Client Repository Fetching, and 32 Client Configuration and Registration—many major dimensions combine unrelated decision points. Split 20 Repository Storage Representation into storage representation versus serving/placement choices, moving values such as 20.2, 20.3, 20.12, and 20.16 accordingly. Split 10 Authority Synchronization into authoritative persistence/serialization versus WAL ingestion, deployment, and compaction, moving 10.4 to 26 Replica Write Commitment Policy and related compaction values to 21 Packfile Lifecycle Management. Split 14 Replica Failure Recovery into failure detection and replica repair/reconstruction; values 14.1, 14.4-14.8, and 14.10 answer detection, while 14.2, 14.3, 14.11, and 14.12 answer repair. Split 11 Repository Serving Architecture into server-side repository serving and client protocol/cache choices, moving 11.4-11.6 to the client-side grouping. Finally, 25 Replica Commit Coordination mixes coordination alternatives with scheduling optimization: move 25.7 to 18 Replica Update Scheduling, and narrow 17 Repository Replication Mechanism by moving materialization and compaction-related values such as 17.9 and 17.10 to the existing serving and packfile dimensions.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Statuses are present and most outcome values describe effects rather than alternatives, with no clear duplicate candidates under different statuses. However, many mixed candidates are described as straightforwardly adopted: 8.2 Scalar performance layer, 12.2 Virtualized filesystem materialization, 17.5 Packfile-level replication, 20.4 Plain Git repositories on local NVMe, 20.5 Normal on-disk Git repository operations, 20.6 Eventually consistent repository replicas, 20.9 Distributed key-value object storage, 27.2 Background Git maintenance, 31.1 Git-aware filesystem watcher, and 31.2 Watchman filesystem watching. Revise each description to state the sources' disagreement or partial adoption, or change the status to accepted where the option was actually adopted. The same issue appears for 6.4 Rolling reboot testing and 10.6 External relational database for repository references, whose mixed statuses also need descriptions that do not imply unqualified adoption.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under existing dimensions. Scalar configuration, core-Git transition, GVFS/partial clone, sparse checkout, background fetching, maintenance, indexing, and filesystem monitoring map to dimensions 8, 12, 22, 27, 28, 30, and 31. Spokes replication, quorum/three-phase coordination, update prioritization, topology, WAL authority, failure recovery, and planned quiescing map to dimensions 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 17, 18, and 25–26. Storage and packfile alternatives are covered by dimensions 11, 20, and 21. No passage remains unplaceable, so no corrective issue is needed.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most explicit choices, including three-phase and majority commits, application-level and geographically distributed replication, quiescing and rolling reboots, background fetch and maintenance, partial clone, sparse checkout, and nested source directories. Missing or insufficiently explicit options should be added: value 'Chaos Monkey testing' to dimension 6 'Maintenance Transition Strategy' as rejected, supported by s03_p08; value 'Loose-object cleanup' to dimension 21 'Packfile Lifecycle Management', supported by s05_p12; value 'VFS for Git background maintenance' to dimension 8 'Client Scaling Integration' (or the relevant maintenance dimension), supported by s05_p09; and value 'Built-in Git File System Monitor' to dimension 31 'Client Filesystem and Status Monitoring', supported by s04_p02.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: All eight dimensions ask distinct architectural questions: coordination protocol (1), replication count (2), state verification (3), authority location (4), request placement (5), server maintenance transitions (6), client maintenance timing (7), and client integration strategy (8). Related values such as S3-backed authority and warm-cache placement, or background maintenance and Scalar/core-Git integration, address different questions rather than duplicating dimensions, so no merge or value move is required under the overlap criterion.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions and values use concrete labels with descriptions that distinguish accepted choices from outcomes, covering both server-side replication/placement and client-side maintenance relevant to very large repositories and many users. Key revisions are needed: dimension 2, "Replication Factor," has nearly indistinguishable values 2.1 "Three replicas per repository" and 2.2 "Three-replica minimum"; merge them or make the fixed-versus-minimum distinction explicit. Dimensions 1 "Replica Commit Coordination" and 4 "Repository Authority Model" have descriptions that are too broad or do not match all values: 1.1 is a protocol choice while 1.2 and 1.3 are consequences, and 4.4 "S3 compare-and-swap synchronization" is a synchronization mechanism rather than an authority-location option; rename or reorganize these dimensions around the questions their values actually answer. In dimension 5, values 5.1 "Rendezvous-hashed repository placement" and 5.2 "Repository-ID and healthy-node routing" substantially overlap and should be merged or differentiated by their static-versus-health-aware behavior. In dimension 7, value 7.2 "Hidden remote-reference namespace" describes reference organization rather than foreground/background execution, so move it to a dimension whose question covers namespace or rename the dimension to encompass that choice.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers several major server and client areas, especially maintenance transition (6), client scaling integration (8), repository placement (5), and client maintenance (7). However, several important decision points do not provide multiple genuine candidate alternatives: Replica Commit Coordination (1) has only accepted 1.1, while 1.2 and 1.3 are outcomes; Replication Factor (2) repeats essentially the same three-replica choice in 2.1 and 2.2, with 2.3 also an outcome; and Replica State Verification (3) mixes implementation details with outcome values rather than presenting alternatives. Reorganize by removing outcome values from candidate lists and merge or drop dimensions 1 and 2 unless their existing values can be reframed as distinct alternatives. Repository Authority Model (4) and Repository Placement Strategy (5) likewise list several adopted mechanisms, but do not clearly identify alternative choices; separate the existing mechanisms into decision questions only where each resulting question retains at least two candidate values.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: All eight dimensions are within scope: dimensions 1–6 address hosting-server decisions for replication, repository authority, placement, consistency, and maintenance at scale, while dimensions 7–8 address client-side fetching, commit-graph maintenance, and large-repository integration. Their decisions concern architectural alternatives or resulting scalability effects for very many repositories, large repositories, and many users. No dimension is clearly outside the stated subject, lifecycle, or decision kind, so no reorganization is needed for scope.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No dimension or value is a catch-all bucket. The dimensions are specific decision points, such as “Replica Commit Coordination” (1), “Repository Placement Strategy” (5), and “Client Maintenance Execution” (7), and their values describe concrete alternatives or outcomes. Broad-sounding items like “Core Git performance capabilities” (8.3) and “Additional Git management layers” (8.4) remain tied to the specific client-scaling integration decision rather than serving as miscellaneous categories.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy uses the required JSON structure and generally distinguishes candidate values from outcomes, but several dimensions combine multiple decision points or contain values that are not alternatives to the stated question. Dimension 3, "Replica State Verification," mixes the checksum design (3.1) with its maintenance strategy (3.2); reorganize these into separate decision dimensions or make 3.1 and 3.2 alternatives under one explicit question. Dimension 4, "Repository Authority Model," combines authority storage (4.1), server statelessness (4.2), primary/consensus policy (4.3), and S3 synchronization (4.4); split or regroup these into distinct questions. Dimension 5, "Repository Placement Strategy," similarly combines routing (5.1–5.2), rematerialization (5.3), and preferred-node selection (5.4); separate the placement/routing decision from recovery and preference policies. Dimension 7, "Client Maintenance Execution," combines background fetching (7.1), reference namespace design (7.2), and commit-graph maintenance (7.3); reorganize each as its own decision where the existing alternatives support it. Dimension 8, "Client Scaling Integration," mixes the architectural choice between Scalar and core Git (8.2–8.3) with build dependency and migration details (8.1, 8.5); move those implementation/transition values to a separately framed existing decision or make the dimension question specifically about integration and transition.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: The output has valid JSON structure and some coherent decision points, but it substantially violates the requirement that each dimension represent one question with at least two candidate alternatives. Dimension 1, "Replica Commit Coordination," has only one candidate: 1.1; 1.2 and 1.3 are outcomes, so dimension 1 should be dropped or its coordination value reorganized into a dimension with other coordination alternatives. Dimension 2's 2.1 and 2.2 are effectively the same three-replica choice rather than alternatives; merge the duplicate and drop dimension 2 if no second existing replication-factor option remains. Dimension 4 combines authority location, stateless serving, primary ownership, and S3 synchronization; retain 4.1-4.2 as the authority model and move 4.3-4.4 into a broadened coordination decision with dimension 1. Dimension 5 mixes placement, routing, materialization, and preferred-primary behavior; move 5.3 to the stateless/cache authority decision and retain the routing-related values together. Dimension 7 similarly combines background fetching, reference namespace organization, and commit-graph maintenance, while dimension 8 combines Scalar dependency, integration layering, and migration; these should be consolidated or have their odd values moved, rather than left as broad multi-question dimensions. The descriptions do reflect scale, availability, latency, and user-waiting concerns, but that does not compensate for the taxonomy's many mixed questions and singleton candidate sets.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: All values use valid statuses, and the descriptions align with them: accepted approaches such as three-phase commit (1.1), S3-backed authority (4.1), and background fetching (7.1) are described as adopted; rejected options 6.1 and 8.4 are explicitly framed as rejected; and outcome values such as replica latency (1.2) and foreground-fetch overhead (7.4) describe effects rather than alternatives. No candidate is repeated under different statuses, and no outcome is presented as a choice.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: Of 19 decision-bearing passages (excluding the introductory rename passage s03_p01), 13 can be mapped, including Scalar/background maintenance under dimensions 7 and 8 and planned maintenance under dimension 6. The unplaced decisions are s02_p02 and s02_p01 (geographically distant replica placement and nearest-replica reads), s02_p06 (coalescing/bookkeeping-update priority and geo-replica behavior), and s01_p03, s01_p04, s01_p05 (choosing distributed filesystems, distributed packfiles, or RPC/dedicated fileservers). Add a replica geography/read-routing dimension with values supported by s02_p01, s02_p02, and s02_p06; add a reference-update scheduling value to dimension 1, “Replica Commit Coordination,” for coalescing and prioritization from s02_p06; and add a server-side repository storage architecture dimension covering filesystem replication, packfile distribution, and dedicated-fileserver RPC, supported by s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers several central choices, including three-phase commit (1.1), three replicas (2.1), S3/WAL authority and rendezvous placement (4.x/5.x), quiescing (6.2), background fetch and commit-graph maintenance (7.1/7.3), and Scalar/core-Git integration (8.x). However, many adopted or rejected options in the passages are unnamed: add a new clone strategy dimension with partial clone versus GVFS, sparse-checkout, and the /src layout, supported by s04_p01, s04_p02, and s05_p04; extend dimension 7, Client Maintenance Execution, with index compression, File System Monitor, multi-pack-index, loose-object cleanup, and incremental background GC, supported by s04_p02, s05_p09, and s05_p12; add a replication architecture dimension for application-level Git replication versus filesystem/block replication, distributed packfiles, object-level DHT, and dedicated-fileserver RPC, supported by s02_p01, s01_p03, s01_p04, and s01_p05; add update/read policy values for coalescing bookkeeping updates, prioritizing user updates, nearest-replica reads, and non-voting geo-replicas, supported by s02_p06; and add resilience/maintenance-policy values for consistency-plus-partition priority with refused writes, rolling quiesced reboots versus chaos testing, rack availability zones, and retirement-time replica repair, supported by s03_p02, s03_p08, and s03_p09.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions, such as checksum strategy (3), maintenance transitions (6), client clone materialization (12), and replica failure recovery (14). However, several values cross decision boundaries: 13.3 Distributed filesystem architecture overlaps the serving/storage-access question in 11 and should move to 11 alongside 11.3 Dedicated repository fileservers; 9.4 Block-level filesystem replication is a storage-replication mechanism rather than a topology/factor choice and should move to 13; and 5.3 Warm-cache materialization overlaps 11.1 Stateless repository-serving cluster, so the warm-cache materialization content should be consolidated under one of those dimensions. These reorganizations would leave one clearer question per affected dimension without merging genuinely different concerns.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Many dimensions have clear decision-oriented names, such as 3 Replica Checksum Strategy, 9 Replica Topology and Factor, and 12 Client Clone Materialization, and most values are distinguishable. However, several descriptions do not define the value they label: 13.8 Incremental pack-file repacking, 13.9 Multi-pack-index reference redirection, and 13.10 Deferred obsolete-pack deletion are phrased as questions rather than descriptions; rewrite them as declarative definitions. The same problem affects 14.4 MxN failure-detection matrix, 14.5 Per-application-server failure isolation, 14.8 Advisory replica-offline status, and 14.9 Cross-server fault inference; replace their question-form text with descriptions matching their labels. Also fix question-form or mismatched entries 1.24 Repository copies as consensus source, 5.6 Routing-database availability dependency, 8.7 GVFS Protocol in standard Git, and 11.10 Horizontal application-server replication by making each description state the corresponding mechanism or outcome. Dimension 7 Client Maintenance Execution has a description focused only on foreground versus background execution while several values concern index formats, filesystem watchers, endpoints, and configuration; revise the description to cover the client-maintenance mechanisms represented by its values.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy represents the major decisions implied by scaling Git across very many repositories, very large repositories, many users, servers, and clients. Server-side areas include replication coordination (1), placement (5), maintenance (6), topology and replica factor (9), authority synchronization (10), serving architecture (11), storage representation (13), and failure recovery (14); client-side areas include maintenance (7), scaling integration (8), and clone materialization (12). Each is supported by multiple candidate values, including accepted and rejected alternatives such as three-phase versus consensus-based replication in dimension 1, block-level replication rejected in 9.4 versus application-level approaches, Watchman rejected in 7.8 versus Git-aware watching, and external relational storage rejected in 10.6 versus an S3-backed WAL.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions directly address the stated scope of scaling Git repositories across hosting servers and clients, including replication and coordination (1, 3, 9, 10), placement and recovery (5, 11, 14), server maintenance (6), and large-repository client behavior (7, 8, 12, 13). The main scope issue is dimension 15, "Version-Control Operating Model": distributed workflows, offline work, and centralized hosting describe collaboration policy rather than architectural decisions for scaling repositories; drop dimension 15. Within dimension 7, value 7.14, "Performance bottleneck tracing," is an investigative practice rather than a hosting or client architecture decision; move it out of the taxonomy or drop it. The remaining dimensions are substantially relevant to the requested server/client scaling context.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No dimension or value is explicitly a catch-all bucket such as “Other,” “Miscellaneous,” or “General considerations.” The taxonomy uses specific names throughout, including “Replica Checksum Strategy,” “Repository Placement Strategy,” and concrete alternatives such as “Rendezvous-hashed repository placement” and “S3-backed write-ahead log.” No catch-all needs to be renamed, split, moved, merged, or dropped.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy extensively combines multiple decision points. Dimension 1, "Replica Commit Coordination," mixes transaction protocol, quorum/consensus, replication mechanism, update scheduling, consistency, and packfile fan-out; split it into separate decision dimensions while retaining the existing alternatives under the matching questions. Dimension 7, "Client Maintenance Execution," similarly combines background fetching, commit-graph/index maintenance, filesystem watching, configuration, status behavior, and cleanup; split these into distinct decision questions. Dimension 13, "Repository Storage Representation," combines repository storage/access representation with pack-repacking and pack-deletion strategy; split those decisions. Dimension 11, "Repository Serving Architecture," combines serving topology, RPC/fileserver access, caching, and client protocol choices; separate these questions. Several values are questions or subtopics rather than alternatives, including 1.24 "Repository copies as consensus source," 5.6 "Routing-database availability dependency," 11.10 "Horizontal application-server replication," and 13.8-13.10; move each into an appropriate decision dimension as an actual candidate or remove the malformed value.

criteria.reason: The taxonomy contains many broad dimensions whose accepted or rejected values answer different questions. Dimension 1, "Replica Commit Coordination," mixes commit protocols (1.1, 1.5, 1.17, 1.20), replication mechanisms (1.6, 1.7, 1.18, 1.19, 1.21), update scheduling (1.8, 1.9), and topology/authority choices (1.4, 1.10, 1.24); split these into decision points with at least two existing candidates and move topology values to 9 and authority values to 10. Dimension 5, "Repository Placement Strategy," mixes hashing, routing, primary selection, read routing, and cache materialization; separate placement/routing while moving 5.3 to the serving/materialization decision. Dimension 7, "Client Maintenance Execution," combines background execution, indexes, filesystem watchers, fetch endpoints, configuration, status behavior, and operational tracing; split execution timing from client acceleration and move 7.10 to the relevant serving/protocol dimension. Dimension 11 mixes stateless deployment, RPC/fileserver architecture, cache-server choices, Git/GVFS protocols, and application scaling; reorganize these into separate existing decision questions, ensuring each retains at least two candidates. Similar mixing occurs in dimensions 6, 9, 12, 14, and 15: for example, 14 combines failure detection, repair, fault inference, and the pet-style operating model, while 15 combines version-control model, workflow, offline use, and hosting. These extensive mixed-question dimensions substantially weaken alignment despite several individually coherent areas such as dimension 10.

Split 11 Repository Serving Architecture into server-side repository serving and client protocol/cache choices, moving 11.4-11.6 to the client-side grouping. Finally, 25 Replica Commit Coordination mixes coordination alternatives with scheduling optimization: move 25.7 to 18 Replica Update Scheduling, and narrow 17 Repository Replication Mechanism by moving materialization and compaction-related values such as 17.9 and 17.10 to the existing serving and packfile dimensions.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Statuses are present and most outcome values describe effects rather than alternatives, with no clear duplicate candidates under different statuses. However, many mixed candidates are described as straightforwardly adopted: 8.2 Scalar performance layer, 12.2 Virtualized filesystem materialization, 17.5 Packfile-level replication, 20.4 Plain Git repositories on local NVMe, 20.5 Normal on-disk Git repository operations, 20.6 Eventually consistent repository replicas, 20.9 Distributed key-value object storage, 27.2 Background Git maintenance, 31.1 Git-aware filesystem watcher, and 31.2 Watchman filesystem watching. Revise each description to state the sources' disagreement or partial adoption, or change the status to accepted where the option was actually adopted. The same issue appears for 6.4 Rolling reboot testing and 10.6 External relational database for repository references, whose mixed statuses also need descriptions that do not imply unqualified adoption.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under existing dimensions. Scalar configuration, core-Git transition, GVFS/partial clone, sparse checkout, background fetching, maintenance, indexing, and filesystem monitoring map to dimensions 8, 12, 22, 27, 28, 30, and 31. Spokes replication, quorum/three-phase coordination, update prioritization, topology, WAL authority, failure recovery, and planned quiescing map to dimensions 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 17, 18, and 25–26. Storage and packfile alternatives are covered by dimensions 11, 20, and 21. No passage remains unplaceable, so no corrective issue is needed.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers most explicit choices, including three-phase and majority commits, application-level and geographically distributed replication, quiescing and rolling reboots, background fetch and maintenance, partial clone, sparse checkout, and nested source directories. Missing or insufficiently explicit options should be added: value 'Chaos Monkey testing' to dimension 6 'Maintenance Transition Strategy' as rejected, supported by s03_p08; value 'Loose-object cleanup' to dimension 21 'Packfile Lifecycle Management', supported by s05_p12; value 'VFS for Git background maintenance' to dimension 8 'Client Scaling Integration' (or the relevant maintenance dimension), supported by s05_p09; and value 'Built-in Git File System Monitor' to dimension 31 'Client Filesystem and Status Monitoring', supported by s04_p02.
